name: Vera Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Can you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a haul truck at the copper pit, one of the big 240-tonne ones, so the tyres alone are twice my height. Day shift I'm up at half four, bus out to the mine at quarter to six, pre-start checks, then it's twelve hours of loop: down the ramp, under the shovel, back up full to the crusher, dump, do it again. Maybe thirty loads on a good day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the radio chatter and I like that I'm good at it. I know every corner of that ramp, where it gets slippery after rain, where the berm's been knocked about. What wears me out is nights, the third night in a row when your eyes go funny around 3 a.m. and you're just counting loads. And the fatigue camera in the cab beeping at you every time you rub your eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds like what my brother-in-law keeps saying, that it's all a bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At smoko everyone's been talking about robots for years, and the trucks are still driven by us. I'd probably say that online too, not that I post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it'd be a relief, but it wouldn't change the main thing I worry about. The driverless trucks at the Kestrel pit down the road don't need clever AI, they just need GPS and money. So even if AI is hype, my job's still on a list somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep driving, keep putting a bit away each pay, keep my union dues paid. I've got about four months saved and I'd like to get it to six before Sami and I look at a place of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest, and still with that little itch about the trucks next door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the Kestrel pit. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They brought in a fleet of driverless trucks about three years back. My mate Josie drove there, and they offered her a job in the control room or a payout. She took the payout and now she drives a school bus, and she says she misses the noise of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So in this picture, what's the one thing you'd still be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether our company signs the same contract Kestrel did. I'd be watching the noticeboard and the union newsletter. If AI is hype, fine, but the truck companies aren't hype, I've seen their trucks with my own eyes.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, because people have been talking about robots for years and the trucks are still driven by us. I'd mostly say it at smoko rather than online.
S0.think: Privately I think it changes less than people assume, because driverless haul trucks don't need clever AI, just GPS and money. Even if AI is hype, my job is still on a list somewhere.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeps paying union dues. Puts a bit away each pay to grow her four months of savings towards six before she and her partner look for a place of their own.
S0.feel: Mostly calm and a little smug, with a background itch about the driverless trucks at the pit next door.
S0.quote: If AI is hype, fine, but the truck companies aren't hype, I've seen their trucks with my own eyes.
S0.fieldNote: Her fear isn't about thinking AI at all; it's anchored in a real fleet of driverless trucks at a nearby pit and a friend who took the payout. That means even the calm scenario carries a specific, local threat. She tracks it through the union newsletter rather than any tech news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one that actually sounds like real life to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union has to get ahead of it, and I'd say it loudly. If tasks are shifting, then workers need a say in which ones and who gets trained. I'd be the one at the meeting asking the site manager to put it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think haul driving is one of the first things to go in that picture. They'll call it a gradual rollout, two trucks, then ten, then the whole fleet. And I'm not the type who'd thrive in a control room staring at screens all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal that guarantees retraining and redeployment, not just payouts. I'd stop the takeaway nights and get my savings from four months to six as fast as I can. And I'd probably ask about moving onto the shovel or a grader, something they'll automate later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicky, because I've got time and some money, but there's a knot there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't thrive in a control room. What would that be like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josie told me about it. You sit at a desk with six screens and watch trucks you used to drive, and you only step in when one gets confused by a puddle. I don't even like using the self-checkout at the supermarket, so you can imagine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Theo, who's been driving for twenty-six years and is two years off his pension. And the younger ones who just bought utes on finance. I'm somewhere in the middle, no kids, no huge loan, so I'd want the union to fight for the ones with more to lose.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to get ahead of it and make sure workers have a say in which tasks change and who gets trained. I'd be the one asking the site manager to put it in writing.
S1.think: I think haul driving is one of the first jobs to go, rolled out a few trucks at a time until it's the whole fleet. I'm also not the kind of person who'd do well in a control room staring at screens.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and pushes for retraining and redeployment rather than payouts. Cuts takeaway nights to grow her savings from four to six months, and asks about moving to the shovel or a grader.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach, though steadied by having some time and some savings.
S1.quote: I don't even like using the self-checkout at the supermarket, so you can imagine.
S1.fieldNote: She sees the union as her main lever, and frames herself as someone who should fight for colleagues with more to lose. Her dislike of screens is real and she says it with humour, but it narrows the options she'll consider. Moving to a different machine is her instinct, not learning a new kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quicker than my lease on the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that a company can make record profits off our backs and then swap us out in two years flat. I'd say the government needs to step in. I'd probably even post that, which tells you how angry I'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out of a job before I've finished paying off the car. Driving a truck is the easiest bit of mining to hand to a robot, they're halfway there already. Two years isn't long enough for me to learn anything new, not at the speed I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cut everything, gym, takeaways, the streaming, and stop the house deposit plan dead. I'd be at the union office pushing for a strike or at least a big redundancy fund, and I'd write to our local member, which I've never done. If the job goes, Sami and I would lean on his parents and the unemployment benefit while I worked out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the floor of the cab dropping out. I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning actually give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Enough to save maybe two more months and feel angry about it. It's not enough to get a trade, an apprenticeship is four years, and I'd be competing with every other driver in the region for the same handful of jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Sami's parents. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. His mum would be lovely about it and that would make it worse. I've been paying my own way since I was seventeen, and I'd hate sitting at their table knowing they're covering the groceries.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disgrace that a company can make record profits off workers and then replace them in two years flat. I'd say the government needs to step in, and I'd probably even post it.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of a job before I'd paid off the car, because driving is the easiest part of mining to automate. Two years isn't enough for me to learn something new at the pace I learn.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, takeaways and streaming in the first month and stops saving for a house deposit. Pushes the union for a strike or redundancy fund, writes to her local member of parliament, and leans on her partner's parents and unemployment benefits if the job goes.
S2.feel: Sick and shaken, like the floor dropping away, and lying awake running numbers.
S2.quote: Two years isn't long enough for me to learn anything new, not at the speed I learn.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her resistance to change and her exposed job collide. She sees two years as only enough time to save and get angry, not to retrain. The thought of accepting help from her partner's family hurt her more than the money itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a bit different, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about the companies, but I'd add that five years is enough time to do this properly. Retraining, a fund paid for by the mining companies, proper notice. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years means I've got no excuse. I'd hate it, but I'd have to start something. The worry is that whatever I pick, the robots get there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and save hard for the first year, aiming for eight months saved instead of four. I'd ask the union to get the company to pay for apprenticeships, and I'd probably apply for an electrical one, because someone has to fix the robots, at least for a while. And I'd vote for whoever promises a tax on the companies doing the replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but with something to hold on to. Alarmed comes and goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical, out of everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's a sparky, so I grew up with it. I know what a multimeter is and I'm not scared of a switchboard. It's hands-on, I'd be on my feet, and it's not staring at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said whatever you pick, the robots get there too. Does that stop you starting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It nearly does, if I'm honest. That's my whole problem, I'd rather sit still and hope. But five years is long enough that sitting still would just be stupid, and I'd know it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly, with retraining, proper notice and a fund paid for by the mining companies. I'd say it at the union meeting and at the pub.
S3.think: I think five years takes away my excuses, so I'd have to start something even though I'd hate it. I also worry that whatever I pick, the robots will reach it too.
S3.do: Keeps driving while saving towards eight months of expenses in the first year. Pushes the union for company-funded apprenticeships, applies for an electrical apprenticeship, and votes for a tax on firms that replace workers.
S3.feel: Anxious but with something to hold on to, and alarmed in waves.
S3.quote: That's my whole problem, I'd rather sit still and hope.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turns her from protest to a reluctant plan, built on her father's trade so it feels familiar. She was candid that her instinct is to sit still and hope. She still channels most of her energy through the union and the ballot box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind when there's a decade's notice. I'd want the union and the government sitting down now, not in year nine. That's what I'd say to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years almost makes it easier to ignore, and that scares me a bit. I know myself. I'd tell myself I've got heaps of time, and then it's 2034 and I'm still on the ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a deadline: start the electrical apprenticeship within two years, while I can still do some truck shifts. I'd keep saving and probably go ahead with buying a small place with Sami, since there's time to pay some of it off. And I'd keep pushing at the union so the company pays for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More worried about my own habits than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by the time it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have my ticket as an electrician, have the place partly paid off, and maybe have a kid by then, but that's a big maybe. I'd want to be the one fixing the trucks, not the one they replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you looked back from 2036, what would you be kicking yourself about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting. Spending eight years saying I'd start next year. I watched my dad stay in one job until it broke his back, and I'd hate to do the same thing just because I was scared of a classroom.

S4.say: I'd say no one should be left behind when there's a decade's notice. I'd want the union and the government sitting down now rather than in year nine.
S4.think: I think ten years almost makes it easier to ignore, which scares me. I know I'd tell myself I have plenty of time and then still be on the ramp years later.
S4.do: Sets herself a deadline to start an electrical apprenticeship within two years while still doing some truck shifts. Keeps saving, goes ahead with buying a small place with her partner, and pushes the union to make the company pay for training.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more worried about her own habit of putting things off than about the robots.
S4.quote: I'd want to be the one fixing the trucks, not the one they replaced.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she becomes her own main risk, and says so. She sets a deadline precisely because she distrusts her habit of waiting. Family plans, including a house and possibly a child, come back on the table only in this scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is the company being forced to pay for retraining before they bring in a single driverless truck, and some kind of income while I'm doing it, so I'm not asking Sami's mum for grocery money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. It's the people on the radio at 3 a.m., talking rubbish to keep each other awake. A robot truck doesn't need anyone to talk to, and I think that's sad for the pit, not just for me.

headlineQuote: A robot truck doesn't need anyone to talk to, and I think that's sad for the pit, not just for me.
portrait: Vera is a 27-year-old haul truck driver at a large open-pit copper mine, living with her partner Sami and holding about four months of savings. She's a loyal union member who distrusts the mining companies and dislikes screens and new technology, which she admits with some humour. Her fear is concrete: a nearby pit already runs driverless trucks. She stays calm in the plateau, turns anxious and union-minded as change speeds up, and is alarmed by AGI in two years, when she sees no time to retrain. With five or ten years she reluctantly plans an electrical apprenticeship in her father's trade, and worries mostly about her own habit of putting things off.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose her driving job before she could learn anything new.
whatWouldHelp: Forcing the company to pay for retraining before any driverless trucks arrive, plus an income while she trains so she doesn't depend on her partner's family.
